items.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Insurance
items.description:
• Origin: Insurance originated in Rhodes (ancient Greece) where merchants pooled sea-voyage risks.
• Definition: Insurance is a risk transfer mechanism where financial losses of few are shared among many through premiums.
• Insurance vs Assurance: Insurance = for events that MAY happen (fire, accident); Assurance = for events that WILL happen (death). Life policies use 'Assurance'.
• Pure Risk vs Speculative Risk: Only PURE RISK (loss or no loss) is insurable. Speculative risk (profit or loss) is NOT insurable.
• Law of Large Numbers: Larger the pool of similar risks, more accurate and predictable the loss estimation.
• Insurer = Company providing coverage. Insured/Assured = Person covered. Premium = Price paid for coverage.
• IRDAI: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India — established under IRDA Act, 1999.
• Insurance reduces uncertainty; it does NOT eliminate risk.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Insurance originated from which place? → Rhodes (Greek island)
Q2. Which type of risk is insurable? → Pure Risk
Q3. What is the difference between Insurance and Assurance? → Insurance is for uncertain events; Assurance is for certain events like death.
Q4. IRDAI was established under which Act? → IRDA Act, 1999
Q5. Does insurance eliminate risk? → NO. It only transfers and reduces the financial impact of risk.

items.title: Chapter 2: Core Elements of Insurance
items.description:
• Asset and Risk: An insurable asset must have economic value and must be exposed to a risk that can cause financial loss.
• Peril: The CAUSE of loss (e.g., fire, flood, accident, death).
• Hazard: A condition that INCREASES the chance of peril occurring.
• Physical Hazard: Relates to physical condition (e.g., bad health, dangerous occupation, faulty wiring).
• Moral Hazard: Relates to dishonesty or fraudulent intention (e.g., insuring overvalued property with intent to claim).
• Morale Hazard: Carelessness or indifference due to having insurance (e.g., not locking car because it is insured).
• Adverse Selection: High-risk individuals are MORE likely to seek insurance than low-risk individuals — insurer must carefully assess.
• Risk Pooling: All policyholders pay premiums into a common pool; claims of a few are paid from this pool.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is a 'Peril'? → The cause/event that leads to a loss (e.g., fire, flood).
Q2. A person does not lock his car because it is insured. This is an example of? → Morale Hazard
Q3. A person takes insurance with the intention of committing fraud. This is? → Moral Hazard
Q4. High-risk individuals seeking more insurance than low-risk individuals is called? → Adverse Selection
Q5. What is the difference between Peril and Hazard? → Peril is the cause of loss; Hazard is a condition increasing the chance of peril.

items.title: Chapter 3: Principles of Insurance
items.description:
• Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei): Both insurer and insured MUST disclose ALL material facts. Concealment or misrepresentation makes the policy VOIDABLE.
• Insurable Interest: The insured must have a financial stake in the subject matter. In Life Insurance, insurable interest must exist AT THE TIME OF TAKING the policy.
• Indemnity: Restore insured to same financial position as before loss — no profit from insurance. Life Insurance is NOT a contract of indemnity (as life cannot be valued).
• Subrogation: After paying a claim, insurer steps into insured's shoes to recover from the liable third party. Subrogation does NOT apply to Life Insurance.
• Contribution: When multiple policies cover the same risk, each insurer contributes proportionally to the claim. Does NOT apply to Life Insurance.
• Proximate Cause: The nearest, immediate, and effective cause of the loss. Claims are settled based on proximate cause.
• Material Fact: Any information that would influence an insurer's decision to accept a risk or fix the premium.
• Warranty: An undertaking by the insured that certain conditions will be fulfilled. Breach of warranty voids the policy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Which Latin term means 'Utmost Good Faith'? → Uberrimae Fidei
Q2. Is Life Insurance a contract of Indemnity? → NO. Life cannot be valued in monetary terms.
Q3. Does Subrogation apply to Life Insurance? → NO. It applies only to General Insurance.
Q4. When must Insurable Interest exist in a Life Insurance policy? → At the time of taking the policy (inception).
Q5. The nearest cause of a loss is called? → Proximate Cause
Q6. When multiple policies cover the same risk, which principle applies? → Contribution

items.title: Chapter 4: Features of Insurance Contracts
items.description:
• Contract of Adhesion: The insured must accept the policy as printed — no room for negotiation of terms.
• Aleatory Contract: The values exchanged are UNEQUAL and depend on chance (insured pays small premium; may receive large claim).
• Conditional Contract: Insurer's obligation to pay a claim depends on fulfillment of certain conditions (e.g., premium payment, disclosure).
• Unilateral Contract: Only the INSURER makes a legally enforceable promise. The insured is not legally bound to pay premiums.
• Personal Contract: The policy is between specific parties and CANNOT be transferred without insurer's consent (except in life insurance by assignment).
• Offer and Acceptance: Proposal form = Offer by proposer. Issuance of policy letter = Acceptance by insurer.
• Consideration: Premium paid by insured is the consideration for the contract.
• Free Look Period: 15 days from receipt of policy to return it if not satisfied (30 days for policies sold via distance marketing like online/telephone).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What type of contract is an insurance contract where the insured cannot negotiate terms? → Contract of Adhesion
Q2. What is the Free Look Period for a regular life insurance policy? → 15 days
Q3. What is the Free Look Period for policies sold through distance marketing? → 30 days
Q4. In an insurance contract, what is the 'Consideration'? → The premium paid by the insured.
Q5. In an insurance contract, who makes the legally enforceable promise? → Only the Insurer (Unilateral contract)

items.title: Chapter 5: Underwriting and Rating
items.description:
• Underwriting: The process of evaluating, selecting, and classifying risks to decide acceptance, rejection, or modified acceptance.
• Standard Life: Normal health and occupation — accepted at standard premium rates.
• Sub-Standard Life: Higher-than-normal risk — accepted with extra premium, reduced sum assured, or exclusion clauses.
• Declined Risk: Risk is too high for the insurer to cover at any premium.
• Key Underwriting Factors for Life Insurance: Age, current health, medical history, family history, occupation, income, habits (smoking/alcohol), residence.
• Moral Hazard: The most critical underwriting concern — dishonest intent or character of the proposer.
• Rating: Determining the appropriate premium for the risk level of the proposer.
• Counter-offer: If insurer accepts at different terms, it is a counter-offer, not acceptance. Proposer must agree to it.
• Numerical Rating System: Assigns numerical debits (extra risk) and credits (favorable factors) to determine overall risk classification.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. A person with higher risk charged extra premium is called? → Sub-Standard Life
Q2. What is the most critical underwriting concern? → Moral Hazard
Q3. What is the process of determining the premium for a given risk called? → Rating
Q4. If the insurer accepts a proposal with different terms, it is called? → Counter-Offer
Q5. Which underwriting system assigns numerical values to risk factors? → Numerical Rating System

items.title: Chapter 6: Claims Processing
items.description:
• Claim: A formal demand by the insured (or nominee/assignee) to the insurer for payment as per policy terms.
• IRDAI Mandate: Insurer MUST settle/reject a claim within 30 days of receiving ALL required documents.
• Investigation Required: If investigation is needed, claim must be settled within 6 MONTHS from date of claim intimation.
• Repudiation: Rejection of a claim by the insurer with valid reasons (e.g., fraud, non-disclosure, policy lapse).
• Surveyor (General Insurance): Appointed for assessing claims above ₹50,000 in general insurance. Must submit report within 30 days.
• Claim Intimation: Must be given to the insurer within the time period mentioned in the policy document.
• Cashless Claims: Insurer directly pays the hospital/service provider (applicable in health/motor insurance).
• Subrogation Arises: AFTER the insurer has paid the claim, subrogation rights transfer to the insurer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Within how many days must a claim be settled after receiving all documents? → 30 days
Q2. If investigation is needed, what is the maximum time to settle a claim? → 6 months from date of intimation
Q3. What is 'Repudiation' of a claim? → Rejection of a claim by the insurer.
Q4. A surveyor must be appointed when the claim amount exceeds? → ₹50,000 (in general insurance)
Q5. When do subrogation rights arise for the insurer? → After the insurer has paid the claim.

items.title: Chapter 7: Documentation
items.description:
• Proposal Form: The MOST IMPORTANT document — it is the basis of the insurance contract. Contains proposer's declarations.
• Policy Document: The legal evidence of the insurance contract issued by the insurer after acceptance.
• KYC Documents: Identity proof (PAN, Aadhaar, Passport, Voter ID, Driving License) and Address proof are mandatory.
• Age Proof — Standard: Birth certificate, Passport, School leaving certificate with date of birth, PAN card.
• Age Proof — Non-Standard: Horoscope, Ration card, Service register, Declaration by parent.
• Income Proof: ITR (Income Tax Return), Salary slip, Form 16 — used to determine appropriate sum assured.
• Assignment Deed: Must be stamped as per the Indian Stamp Act to be legally valid.
• Revival Documents: For lapsed policies — Declaration of Good Health (DGH) + payment of all due premiums with interest.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Which is the most important document that forms the basis of an insurance contract? → Proposal Form
Q2. Is a horoscope a standard or non-standard age proof? → Non-Standard Age Proof
Q3. What documents are needed to revive a lapsed policy? → Declaration of Good Health (DGH) + outstanding premiums with interest
Q4. An assignment deed must be stamped under which Act? → Indian Stamp Act
Q5. What is the primary purpose of income proof in life insurance? → To determine appropriate Sum Assured (prevent over-insurance).

items.title: Chapter 8: Customer Service
items.description:
• Free Look Period: 15 days (30 days for distance/online marketing) to review and return the policy with full premium refund (minus medical/stamp charges).
• Policy Bond Delivery: Must be delivered to the policyholder within 30 DAYS of receiving the first premium.
• Premium Receipt: Must be issued within 3 DAYS of receiving the premium payment.
• Renewal Notice: Insurer must send a renewal reminder at least 30 DAYS before the premium due date.
• Policy Servicing includes: Change of nomination, change of address, mode of premium payment change, assignment, policy revival.
• Grace Period: The time allowed after premium due date for payment without penalty — 30 days (for monthly mode: 15 days).
• Lapsed Policy: If premium not paid within grace period, the policy lapses and coverage ceases.
• Agent's Role: First point of contact for policyholder service; must assist in claims, renewals, and servicing requests.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the grace period for life insurance policies (non-monthly mode)? → 30 days
Q2. What is the grace period for monthly premium payment mode? → 15 days
Q3. Within how many days must the policy bond be delivered? → 30 days from first premium receipt
Q4. How many days before premium due date must the renewal notice be sent? → 30 days
Q5. Within how many days of premium payment must a receipt be issued? → 3 days

items.title: Chapter 9: Grievance Redressal Mechanism (Ombudsman)
items.description:
• IRDAI IGMS: Integrated Grievance Management System — centralized online platform for filing insurance complaints (www.igms.irda.gov.in).
• Insurance Ombudsman: Established under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 (previously Redressal of Public Grievances Rules, 1998).
• Pecuniary Limit: Ombudsman can handle complaints up to ₹30 LAKH (personal lines of insurance).
• Who Can Complain: Any individual policyholder, nominee, or assignee — NOT corporate entities.
• Pre-condition: Must first complain to insurer and either get a rejection OR no response within 30 DAYS.
• Time Limit to Approach Ombudsman: Within 1 YEAR of insurer's final reply or 1 year of rejection.
• Ombudsman Award: Recommendation within 30 days (for conciliation); final Award within 3 MONTHS of receipt of complaint.
• Number of Ombudsman Offices: 17 across India.
• If insured disagrees with award: Can approach civil court. If insured accepts: Insurer MUST comply within 30 DAYS.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the monetary limit of the Insurance Ombudsman? → ₹30 Lakh
Q2. Within how many days must the insurer respond to a grievance before approaching Ombudsman? → 30 days
Q3. Within how many months does the Ombudsman give a final Award? → 3 months
Q4. Within what time limit from insurer's reply can you approach Ombudsman? → 1 year
Q5. Can a corporate entity approach the Insurance Ombudsman? → NO. Only individual policyholders, nominees, or assignees.
Q6. What is IGMS? → Integrated Grievance Management System — IRDAI's centralized complaint portal.

items.title: Chapter 10: Regulatory Aspects for Insurance Agents
items.description:
• IRDAI Act: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India established under IRDA Act, 1999.
• Minimum Age: 18 years to become a licensed insurance agent.
• Educational Qualification: Minimum 12th standard pass (for urban areas/towns with population above 5,000); 10th standard pass (for rural/other areas).
• Mandatory Training: 50 HOURS of practical training from an IRDAI-approved institution.
• License Validity: 3 YEARS. Renewal requires 25 hours of continuing education (CE credits).
• Agency Rule: An agent can represent ONLY ONE life insurer + ONE general insurer + ONE standalone health insurer at the same time.
• Code of Conduct: Must not misrepresent policy features, must disclose commission, cannot rebate premium back to client.
• Rebating is PROHIBITED: Sharing commission or offering inducements to buy a policy is illegal and punishable.
• Principal: The insurance company is the 'Principal'; the agent acts on behalf of the principal.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the minimum age to become an insurance agent? → 18 years
Q2. How many hours of training are mandatory before getting an agent license? → 50 hours
Q3. How long is an insurance agent's license valid? → 3 years
Q4. Can an agent represent two life insurance companies simultaneously? → NO. Only one life insurer at a time.
Q5. What is 'Rebating' and is it allowed? → Sharing commission with client as inducement — it is STRICTLY PROHIBITED.
Q6. How many CE hours are required for license renewal? → 25 hours

items.title: Chapter 11: What Life Insurance Involves
items.description:
• Life Insurance: A contract where insurer promises to pay the Sum Assured on the death of the life assured OR on survival to the end of the policy term.
• Human Life Value (HLV): Method to calculate the economic value of a human life to determine adequate Sum Assured. It is the present value of future net income.
• HLV Factors: Current age, annual income, personal expenses, existing liabilities, number of earning years remaining, expected salary growth.
• Nomination: Appointment of a person (nominee) to receive the policy proceeds in case of death of the life assured. Nominee does NOT need insurable interest.
• Assignment: Transfer of rights, title, and interest in a policy from Assignor (policyholder) to Assignee.
• Absolute Assignment: Transfers ALL rights permanently to the assignee. Cannot be revoked.
• Conditional Assignment: Transfer subject to conditions (e.g., on death of assignor, policy reverts back).
• Rider/Add-on: Additional benefit attached to base life policy for extra protection (e.g., Accidental Death Rider, Waiver of Premium Rider, Critical Illness Rider).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What method is used to determine the appropriate sum assured for a life insurance policy? → Human Life Value (HLV) method
Q2. Does a nominee need to have insurable interest in the life assured? → NO
Q3. What is 'Absolute Assignment'? → Permanent, irrevocable transfer of all policy rights to the assignee.
Q4. What is a 'Rider' in a life insurance policy? → An additional benefit/cover attached to the base policy.
Q5. Who is an 'Assignee'? → The person to whom the policy rights are transferred.

items.title: Chapter 12: Financial Planning
items.description:
• Financial Planning: The process of setting financial goals and creating a systematic plan to achieve them through proper resource management.
• 6 Steps of Financial Planning: (1) Establish client-planner relationship → (2) Gather client data → (3) Analyze and evaluate data → (4) Develop recommendations → (5) Implement the plan → (6) Monitor and review the plan.
• Life Stages & Needs: Young single (risk cover), Young married (family cover + savings), Middle age (children's education, retirement), Pre-retirement (wealth accumulation), Retirement (income generation).
• Need Analysis: Identifying insurance needs based on income, liabilities, number of dependents, future goals.
• Inflation Impact: Reduces purchasing power over time; insurance plans must account for inflation in their coverage amounts.
• Tax Benefits: Premium paid eligible under Section 80C (up to ₹1.5 lakh deduction); Maturity/Death benefit tax-free under Section 10(10D) of Income Tax Act.
• Section 80D: Premium paid for health insurance is deductible — ₹25,000 for self/family; ₹50,000 for senior citizens.
• Risk Tolerance: An investor's ability and willingness to accept variability in investment returns.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. How many steps are there in the financial planning process? → 6 steps
Q2. Under which section is life insurance premium tax-deductible? → Section 80C (up to ₹1.5 lakh)
Q3. Under which section is the death/maturity benefit of life insurance tax-free? → Section 10(10D)
Q4. Under which section is health insurance premium tax-deductible? → Section 80D
Q5. What is 'Need Analysis' in financial planning? → Assessing the client's insurance requirements based on income, liabilities, and dependents.

items.title: Chapter 13: Life Insurance Products — Traditional
items.description:
• Term Insurance: Pure protection plan — pays Sum Assured ONLY on death within policy term. NO maturity benefit. LOWEST premium among all plans.
• Endowment Policy: Pays Sum Assured on DEATH within term OR on SURVIVAL to maturity. Combines protection + savings. Most popular traditional product.
• Whole Life Policy: Provides life cover for the ENTIRE life of insured (typically up to age 99/100). Sum Assured paid on death only.
• Money Back Policy: Pays a percentage of Sum Assured as Survival Benefit at regular intervals during the policy term + balance on maturity.
• Participating (With-Profit) Policy: Eligible for bonuses declared by the insurer from its profits.
• Reversionary Bonus: Declared every year as a % of Sum Assured; added to the policy and paid on claim/maturity.
• Terminal Bonus: One-time bonus paid at the time of claim or maturity (not declared every year).
• Children's Plan: Designed to fund a child's education/marriage; includes payor benefit rider (waiver of premium on parent's death).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Which life insurance plan offers ONLY death benefit with NO maturity benefit? → Term Insurance
Q2. Which plan pays survival benefits at regular intervals during the policy term? → Money Back Policy
Q3. What is a 'Reversionary Bonus'? → Bonus declared each year, added to policy, paid on claim/maturity.
Q4. Which plan provides coverage for the entire life of the insured? → Whole Life Policy
Q5. Which is the CHEAPEST life insurance plan in terms of premium? → Term Insurance
Q6. Which traditional plan is most popular and combines protection + savings? → Endowment Policy

items.title: Chapter 14: Life Insurance Products — Non-Traditional (ULIPs)
items.description:
• ULIP: Unit Linked Insurance Plan — combines Life Insurance protection with Market-Linked investment.
• Premium Split: Part of premium → mortality/insurance charges; remaining part → invested in chosen market funds.
• Lock-in Period: MINIMUM 5 YEARS as per IRDAI regulation. Surrender not allowed before 5 years.
• Fund Types: Equity Fund (high risk, high return), Debt Fund (low risk, low return), Balanced/Hybrid Fund (medium risk and return).
• NAV (Net Asset Value): The price per unit of a ULIP fund. Calculated daily. Higher NAV = more units.
• Key ULIP Charges: Premium Allocation Charge, Policy Administration Charge, Mortality Charge, Fund Management Charge (FMC).
• FMC Cap: Maximum 1.35% per annum of fund value (regulated by IRDAI).
• Partial Withdrawal: Allowed ONLY after the 5-year lock-in period.
• Switching: Transfer units between funds (e.g., equity to debt). Usually 4 free switches per year.
• Top-up Premium: Additional lump-sum premium can be paid to increase investment corpus.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the lock-in period for ULIPs as per IRDAI? → 5 years
Q2. What is 'NAV' in a ULIP? → Net Asset Value — the daily price per unit of the fund.
Q3. What is the maximum Fund Management Charge (FMC) allowed in ULIPs? → 1.35% per annum
Q4. Can partial withdrawal be made from a ULIP within the lock-in period? → NO. Only after 5 years.
Q5. What is 'Switching' in a ULIP? → Transferring investment from one fund to another (e.g., equity to debt).
Q6. Which ULIP fund is most suitable for a risk-averse investor? → Debt Fund

items.title: Chapter 15: Applications of Life Insurance (MWP Act, Keyman)
items.description:
• MWP Act: Married Women's Property Act, 1874 — Section 6 allows a married man to take a life policy for the benefit of wife and/or children.
• MWP Trust: Such a policy creates an automatic TRUST. The proceeds CANNOT be attached by creditors, courts, or even the policyholder himself.
• Trustee: The wife and/or children are the beneficiaries; a trustee manages the trust (can be the wife or a named person).
• Keyman Insurance: A life insurance policy taken by a COMPANY (employer) on the life of a KEY EMPLOYEE whose death would cause financial loss to the business.
• Keyman Policy: Premium paid by employer → Employer is the Proposer, Payer, and Beneficiary. The key employee is the Life Assured only.
• Tax Treatment (Keyman): Premium paid is a TAX-DEDUCTIBLE business expense. Claim received by employer is taxable as business income.
• Assignment of Keyman Policy: Cannot be assigned to the employee while the person is still employed as a keyman (restrictions apply).
• Group Insurance: One MASTER POLICY covers a group of individuals (e.g., employees). Each member gets a Certificate of Insurance (not individual policy).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Under which section of MWP Act can a husband take a policy for wife/children? → Section 6
Q2. Can creditors attach the proceeds of an MWP policy? → NO. It is protected by the automatic trust.
Q3. In Keyman Insurance, who is the beneficiary? → The Employer (Company)
Q4. In Keyman Insurance, who is the Life Assured? → The Key Employee
Q5. Is the Keyman Insurance premium tax deductible? → YES, as a business expense.
Q6. What document does each member of a Group Insurance scheme receive? → Certificate of Insurance (not an individual policy bond).

items.title: Chapter 16: Pricing and Valuation in Life Insurance
items.description:
• Actuary: A specially trained professional who uses mathematics, statistics, and financial theory to calculate insurance premiums, reserves, and valuation.
• Net Premium: Calculated purely on the basis of mortality rate and assumed interest rate — does NOT include expenses.
• Gross Premium (Office Premium): Net Premium + Loading. Loading covers expenses, profit margin, and contingencies.
• Mortality Table (Life Table): Statistical table showing the probability of death at each age — the foundation of life insurance pricing.
• Reserve (Policy Reserve): The amount an insurer sets aside from premiums to meet future claim obligations. Mandatory under IRDAI regulations.
• Surrender Value: Amount paid to the policyholder if they voluntarily terminate the policy BEFORE maturity. Policy acquires surrender value after 3 consecutive years of premium payment.
• Guaranteed Surrender Value (GSV): Minimum surrender value as per IRDAI — typically 30% of total premiums paid (excluding first year) after 3 years.
• Paid-up Value: If a policyholder stops paying premiums (after 3 years), policy becomes 'Paid-up' with reduced Sum Assured proportional to premiums paid.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Who calculates insurance premiums and reserves using actuarial science? → Actuary
Q2. After how many years of premium payment does a policy acquire surrender value? → 3 years
Q3. What is 'Gross Premium'? → Net Premium + Loading (for expenses and profit).
Q4. What is the GSV (Guaranteed Surrender Value) percentage? → 30% of total premiums paid (excluding first year premium) after 3 years.
Q5. What is a 'Paid-up Policy'? → A policy with reduced Sum Assured when the policyholder stops paying premiums (after 3 years).
Q6. What table forms the foundation of life insurance pricing? → Mortality Table (Life Table)

items.title: Chapter 17: Life Insurance Documentation
items.description:
• Proposal Form: The application submitted by the proposer — it is the FOUNDATION of the life insurance contract. All declarations must be true.
• Policy Bond: The physical/digital document issued by insurer as evidence of the contract. Must be delivered within 30 days of first premium.
• Standard Age Proof: Birth certificate, Passport, PAN card, School/College leaving certificate with DOB, Municipal birth record.
• Non-Standard Age Proof: Horoscope, Ration card, Self-declaration, Service register — accepted with age warranty clause (risk of incorrect age falls on insured).
• Nomination: Named person to receive policy proceeds on death. Can be changed any number of times during policy term. Beneficiary nominee vs. collecting nominee.
• Assignment: Must be notified in writing to the insurer. Absolute or Conditional. Assignment deed must be stamped under Stamp Act.
• Revival Process: Lapsed policy can be revived within 5 YEARS from first unpaid premium. Requires: Declaration of Good Health (DGH) + all due premiums + interest.
• Duplicate Policy: Issued when original is lost. Requires an indemnity bond (surety) before duplicate is issued.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Is a horoscope a valid age proof in life insurance? → YES, but it is Non-Standard Age Proof.
Q2. Within how many years can a lapsed policy be revived? → 5 years from the date of first unpaid premium
Q3. What is required to revive a lapsed policy? → Declaration of Good Health (DGH) + all due premiums + interest
Q4. What is needed to issue a duplicate policy? → An Indemnity Bond (surety bond)
Q5. Can nomination be changed once made? → YES, it can be changed any number of times during the policy term.

items.title: Chapter 18: Life Insurance Underwriting
items.description:
• Life Insurance Underwriting: Process of evaluating the risk presented by a proposer to decide acceptance, extra premium, exclusion, or rejection.
• Non-Medical Underwriting: Policy issued without medical examination — applicable for younger ages and lower Sum Assured amounts.
• Medical Underwriting: Medical tests required for high Sum Assured or older age proposers.
• Key Underwriting Factors: Age, gender, medical history, current health status, family history, occupation, lifestyle (smoking, alcohol), BMI, residence.
• Hazardous Occupations: Extra premium charged (e.g., miners, deep-sea divers, pilots, explosives workers) or policy declined.
• Juvenile Underwriting: For children below 7-10 years — risk of adverse selection is higher; special care is taken. Sum Assured may be restricted.
• Free Cover Limit (Group Insurance): Sum Assured up to this limit in group insurance does NOT require individual medical evidence.
• Lien: A restriction placed on a policy for a specific period (e.g., 1-2 years) during which only return of premiums is paid in case of early death (used for sub-standard lives).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is Non-Medical Underwriting? → Issuing a policy without requiring medical tests (for low sum assured/young age).
Q2. What is a 'Lien' in life insurance underwriting? → A restriction during which only premiums paid are refunded in case of early death — for sub-standard lives.
Q3. What is the 'Free Cover Limit' in Group Insurance? → The maximum sum assured below which no individual medical evidence is required.
Q4. For which type of lives is extra premium charged due to dangerous occupations? → Sub-Standard Lives
Q5. What is 'Juvenile Underwriting'? → Special underwriting rules for insuring children's lives.

items.title: Chapter 19: Life Insurance Claims
items.description:
• Maturity Claim: Paid when the life assured SURVIVES to the end of the policy term. Proof of age and original policy bond required.
• Death Claim: Paid on the death of the life assured. Documents: Claim form, Original policy bond, Death certificate, Identity proof of nominee.
• Early Death Claim: Death within 3 YEARS of policy issuance/revival — insurer conducts detailed investigation before settling.
• Non-Early Death Claim: Death AFTER 3 years — simpler process, investigation normally not required.
• IRDAI Regulation: All death claims must be settled within 30 DAYS of receiving all required documents. If investigation needed: within 6 MONTHS of claim intimation.
• Suicide Clause (IRDAI Rule): If life assured commits suicide within 1 YEAR of policy commencement or revival → insurer pays 80% of premiums paid (not full sum assured).
• Presumption of Death: If body cannot be found, a court declaration under Section 108 of Indian Evidence Act is required.
• Annuity Claims: On death of annuitant, the annuity payments stop (for life annuity without return of purchase price).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Death within how many years of policy issuance is called an 'Early Death Claim'? → Within 3 years
Q2. What is paid if suicide occurs within 1 year of policy start/revival? → 80% of premiums paid (not full sum assured)
Q3. Within how many days must a life insurance death claim be settled? → 30 days (after receiving all documents)
Q4. If investigation is needed, what is the maximum time to settle a death claim? → 6 months from claim intimation
Q5. What is needed if the body of the insured is not found for a death claim? → Court declaration under Section 108 of Indian Evidence Act (Presumption of Death)

items.title: Chapter 20: Introduction to Health Insurance
items.description:
• Health Insurance: Insurance that covers financial losses arising from illness, injury, hospitalization, or medical treatment.
• Regulatory Authority: IRDAI regulates all health insurance in India.
• Third Party Administrator (TPA): An IRDAI-licensed intermediary that processes health insurance claims and provides cashless services on behalf of insurers.
• Network Hospital: Hospital that has an agreement with the insurer/TPA to provide CASHLESS treatment to policyholders.
• Non-Network Hospital: Treatment taken here requires REIMBURSEMENT claim (insured pays first, then claims from insurer).
• Pre-Existing Disease (PED): Any medical condition that existed BEFORE the policy was taken.
• PED Waiting Period: Maximum 36 MONTHS (3 years) as per IRDAI regulations.
• Initial Waiting Period: 30 DAYS from policy start date — no claims payable except for accidental injuries.
• Hospitalization Definition: Minimum 24-HOUR admission in a hospital is required for a regular claim (exception: Day Care procedures).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is a TPA in health insurance? → Third Party Administrator — processes claims and cashless services.
Q2. What is the maximum waiting period for Pre-Existing Diseases (PED) as per IRDAI? → 36 months (3 years)
Q3. What is the initial waiting period in health insurance? → 30 days (only accidental claims allowed)
Q4. What is the minimum hospitalization period required for a health insurance claim? → 24 hours
Q5. What is a 'Network Hospital'? → A hospital empanelled with the insurer for cashless treatment.

items.title: Chapter 21: Health Insurance Documentation
items.description:
• Proposal Form: Contains complete health history, lifestyle details, pre-existing conditions, and family medical history of all insured members.
• Health Card / TPA Card: Issued by TPA after policy issuance. Used to avail cashless facility at network hospitals.
• Pre-Authorization Form: Must be submitted to the TPA/insurer BEFORE planned hospitalization for cashless approval. For emergencies, submitted within a few hours of admission.
• Discharge Summary: Hospital document summarizing diagnosis, treatment, and instructions — mandatory for claim processing.
• Claim Form (Reimbursement): Duly filled claim form submitted with all original bills, medical reports, and discharge summary.
• PAN Card: Mandatory for claim settlements ABOVE ₹1 LAKH.
• KYC Documents: Mandatory for all health insurance policies (identity + address proof).
• Investigation Reports: Lab test results, X-ray, CT scan, MRI reports — essential supporting documents for claim.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the purpose of a Pre-Authorization Form? → To get cashless treatment approval from TPA/insurer before hospitalization.
Q2. PAN card is mandatory for health insurance claims above how much amount? → ₹1 Lakh
Q3. Which document issued by the hospital is most important for claim processing? → Discharge Summary
Q4. What is a TPA Health Card used for? → To avail cashless treatment at network hospitals.
Q5. Is the Proposal Form important in health insurance? → YES — it contains health history and forms the basis of risk assessment.

items.title: Chapter 22: Health Insurance Products
items.description:
• Indemnity Plans: Reimburse actual medical expenses incurred (up to Sum Insured). Examples: Mediclaim, Individual Health, Family Floater plans.
• Defined Benefit Plans: Pay a FIXED lump sum on occurrence of a specific event regardless of actual expenses. Examples: Critical Illness, Hospital Daily Cash.
• Family Floater Policy: ONE Sum Insured shared among ALL family members. If one member claims, it reduces the pool for others. CHEAPER than individual policies for each member.
• Critical Illness Policy: Pays lump sum on FIRST DIAGNOSIS of listed critical illnesses (cancer, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, etc.).
• Hospital Daily Cash: Pays a FIXED DAILY AMOUNT for each day of hospitalization irrespective of actual expenses.
• Top-up Policy: Pays claims ABOVE a threshold (deductible). Provides cost-effective higher coverage.
• Super Top-up Policy: Aggregates multiple claims in a year above the deductible threshold — better than regular top-up.
• Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY: Government scheme providing health coverage of ₹5 LAKH per family per year for BPL families.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. Which health insurance plan pays a fixed amount per day of hospitalization? → Hospital Daily Cash
Q2. In a Family Floater policy, how many Sum Insured amounts are there? → ONE — shared by the entire family.
Q3. Critical Illness policy pays on? → First Diagnosis of the listed illness (not on actual expenses).
Q4. What is the coverage amount under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY? → ₹5 Lakh per family per year
Q5. What is the difference between Top-up and Super Top-up? → Top-up activates per individual claim above deductible; Super Top-up considers aggregate claims in a year.
Q6. Which type of health plan pays on actual expenses incurred? → Indemnity Plan

items.title: Chapter 23: Health Insurance Underwriting
items.description:
• Health Insurance Underwriting: Evaluating health risk of the proposer based on medical history, age, lifestyle, and existing conditions.
• Pre-Existing Disease (PED): Condition existing BEFORE policy start. Covered after the waiting period (max 36 months per IRDAI).
• Initial Waiting Period: 30 days from policy commencement — general illnesses not covered; only accidents covered.
• Specific Disease Waiting Period: 1-2 years waiting period for specific conditions like hernia, cataract, joint replacement, etc.
• Co-payment: Insured bears a FIXED PERCENTAGE of each claim (e.g., 20%). Used for senior citizens or higher risk proposers.
• Deductible: A FIXED AMOUNT the insured must pay before insurance kicks in. Reduces premium cost.
• Sub-limit: A CAP on specific expenses like room rent (e.g., 1% of Sum Insured per day), doctor fees, or specific treatments.
• Moratorium Period (IRDAI Rule): After 8 CONTINUOUS YEARS of health insurance coverage, the insurer CANNOT contest any claim on PED grounds (protection for long-term policyholders).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. What is the maximum PED waiting period as per IRDAI? → 36 months (3 years)
Q2. After how many years of continuous health insurance can the insurer NOT contest PED claims? → 8 years (Moratorium Period)
Q3. What is 'Co-payment' in health insurance? → A fixed % of the claim borne by the insured (e.g., 20% co-pay).
Q4. What is a 'Sub-limit' in health insurance? → A cap on specific expenses like room rent or doctor fees.
Q5. What is the initial waiting period in health insurance? → 30 days (only accidental injuries are covered immediately).
Q6. What is a 'Deductible'? → A fixed amount the insured must pay first before the insurer pays.

items.title: Chapter 24: Health Insurance Claims
items.description:
• Cashless Claim: Insurer directly settles the bill with the NETWORK HOSPITAL. Insured does not pay (except for non-covered items). Requires pre-authorization.
• Reimbursement Claim: Insured pays the hospital first, then submits original bills to insurer/TPA for reimbursement.
• Pre-authorization for Cashless: For PLANNED hospitalization — must be applied for in advance. For EMERGENCY — must be submitted within a few hours of admission.
• IRDAI TAT (Turnaround Time): Cashless authorization must be given within 1 HOUR of receiving the request. Final discharge authorization within 3 hours.
• Reimbursement Settlement: Insurer must settle/reject reimbursement claim within 30 DAYS of receiving all documents.
• Day Care Procedures: Medical procedures completed in LESS THAN 24 HOURS due to advanced technology (e.g., dialysis, chemotherapy, cataract surgery). Most policies cover these.
• Claim Rejection Reasons: Non-disclosure of PED, exclusion clause, waiting period, treatment in non-network hospital without approval, non-medical expenses.
• Escalation Path: Insurer's Grievance Cell → IRDAI IGMS Portal → Insurance Ombudsman (if claim ≤ ₹30 lakh) → Civil Court.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📝 FREQUENTLY ASKED MCQs
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Q1. In cashless claim, who pays the hospital directly? → The Insurance Company (through TPA)
Q2. What is the IRDAI turnaround time for cashless pre-authorization? → Within 1 hour of receiving the request
Q3. What are 'Day Care Procedures'? → Medical treatments completed in less than 24 hours due to advanced technology.
Q4. Within how many days must a reimbursement claim be settled? → 30 days of receiving all documents
Q5. What is the escalation path if a health insurance claim is rejected? → Insurer's Grievance Cell → IRDAI IGMS → Insurance Ombudsman → Civil Court
Q6. Can a health insurance claim be rejected for visiting a non-network hospital? → YES, if cashless treatment was taken at a non-network hospital without prior approval.
